title: South Asian Adults in the US Have 30 Per Cent Prediabetes by Age 45. They Also Report the Healthiest Diets. A Major Study Says the Paradox Is Real.
excerpt: The MASALA study followed 2,700 adults for a decade and found that South Asians develop cardiovascular risk factors earlier than every other ethnic group — despite doing many of the right things.
body:
If you are a South Asian adult living in the United States, you have probably heard some version of this advice your entire life: eat well, exercise regularly, avoid alcohol, and your heart will be fine. A major study published in the Journal of the American Heart Association earlier this year suggests that for people of Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi, Nepali, and Sri Lankan descent, doing all the right things may not be enough.

The study, led by Dr. Namratha Kandula at Northwestern University's Feinberg School of Medicine, combined data from two long-running cohort studies — MASALA (Mediators of Atherosclerosis in South Asians Living in America) and MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) — to track cardiovascular risk factors in 2,700 adults aged 45 to 55 over a decade.

The findings are striking. At age 45, South Asian men had a prediabetes prevalence of 30.7 per cent — nearly eight times higher than white men (3.9 per cent) and roughly triple the rate among Black (10.4 per cent), Hispanic (10.5 per cent), and Chinese (12.6 per cent) men. South Asian women fared only slightly better, with 17.6 per cent prediabetes at age 45, still double the rate of every other group studied.

The Paradox That Keeps Researchers Up at Night

What makes this data unusual is not just the scale of the risk. It is the disconnect between lifestyle and outcomes.

South Asian participants in the study reported the highest diet quality scores of any group. They had lower alcohol consumption. Their exercise habits were comparable to peers. By every behavioural measure that public health campaigns emphasise, South Asians were doing well.

Yet by age 55, they were at least twice as likely to have developed type 2 diabetes as white adults of the same age. Hypertension was present in 25.5 per cent of South Asian men at age 45, higher than white (18.4 per cent), Chinese (6.6 per cent), and Hispanic (10.1 per cent) men. Dyslipidemia — abnormal cholesterol and triglyceride levels — affected 78.2 per cent of South Asian men, the highest of any group.

"The mismatch between healthier lifestyle behaviours and clinical risk was surprising," Dr. Kandula told Northwestern News. "This paradox tells us we are missing something fundamental to what is driving this elevated risk among South Asians."

What Is Driving the Risk?

Researchers point to several factors beyond diet and exercise. South Asians tend to accumulate visceral fat — the metabolically active fat around internal organs — at lower body weights than other populations. A person who looks lean by Western BMI standards may be carrying dangerous amounts of abdominal fat. Standard BMI thresholds, developed primarily from European populations, systematically underestimate metabolic risk in South Asians.

There is also growing evidence that insulin resistance develops earlier and more aggressively in people of South Asian descent, driven by a combination of genetic predisposition and epigenetic factors shaped by generations of nutritional patterns. The traditional South Asian diet, while rich in vegetables and whole grains, is also high in refined carbohydrates, fried foods, and saturated fats from ghee and cooking oils — a pattern that may interact with these genetic tendencies.

Inflammatory biomarkers, including C-reactive protein and lipoprotein(a), tend to run higher in South Asian populations. These nontraditional risk factors are not captured by standard screening protocols, which were designed around populations with different risk profiles.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For the estimated five million Indian Americans and the broader South Asian community in the United States, the implications are direct. The American Heart Association published a scientific statement in 2018 specifically addressing atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in South Asians, noting that this population experiences heart attacks a decade earlier than the general population — often before age 60.

The MASALA study adds a critical finding to that picture: the risk window does not begin at 55 or 60. It is already wide open by 45.

"We have now identified a critical window in the 40s when risk is already high, but disease is still preventable," Dr. Kandula said.

For NRI families, this translates into a simple but often neglected action: do not wait for symptoms. Get screened for blood pressure, fasting glucose, HbA1c, and cholesterol in your early 40s — or even your late 30s if you have a family history of diabetes or heart disease. Standard age-based screening guidelines, which often begin at 45 or 50 for the general population, may come too late for South Asians.

What You Can Do Now

The study does not suggest that lifestyle changes are pointless. It suggests they are necessary but not sufficient.

Dr. Kandula's team recommends earlier and more aggressive screening, culturally tailored prevention programmes, and a willingness among physicians to treat South Asian patients at lower BMI thresholds than standard guidelines suggest. The WHO already uses a lower BMI cutoff for overweight in Asian populations (23 kg/m² instead of 25), but this adjustment is not consistently applied in clinical practice in the United States.

For individuals, the practical steps are clear:

  • Get screened earlier. Ask for fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid panel, and blood pressure checks starting in your early 40s. If your doctor says your BMI is normal and moves on, push for the blood work anyway.
  • Watch waist circumference, not just weight. A waist measurement above 90 cm for men or 80 cm for women (WHO Asian-specific cutoffs) is a stronger risk signal than BMI for South Asians.
  • Reduce refined carbohydrates. White rice, naan, and maida-based foods spike blood sugar in ways that interact with South Asian insulin resistance patterns. This does not mean eliminating them — it means being deliberate about portions.
  • Prioritise resistance training. Building muscle mass improves insulin sensitivity. Walking alone, while beneficial, may not be enough to counteract the metabolic predisposition.

The MASALA study is the most comprehensive longitudinal dataset on South Asian cardiovascular health in the United States. It confirms what many in the community have long suspected: the rules of the game are different for us. The question is whether the healthcare system — and our own habits — will adapt quickly enough to make a difference.
